1:7.t: "His holy people": the KJV's "saints". In the New Testament, all believers are "saints" (Greek hagioi), set apart for God, not only a few exceptional people. See Acts 9:13.

1:14.t: "Non-Greeks": the KJV's "Barbarians", those who did not speak Greek.

1:17.t: "The righteousness of God" (Greek dikaiosyne theou): a key phrase in Romans. It can mean God's own righteousness, His faithfulness to His promises, and the right standing He gives to those who believe (3:21-26, 5:17). "By faith from first to last" (Greek ek pisteos eis pistin): the KJV's "from faith to faith", meaning from beginning to end the gospel rests on faith. "Faith" (Greek pistis): trust, reliance, faithfulness.

2:6.t: A quotation of Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12.

2:22.t: "Rob temples": the KJV's "commit sacrilege"; Greek hierosyleo, to rob a temple. See Acts 19:37.

2:24.t: A quotation of Isaiah 52:5 from the Greek.

3:4.t: A quotation of Psalm 51:4 from the Greek. "Not at all!": the KJV's "God forbid"; Greek me genoito, a strong denial, "May it never be!" Also 3:6, 3:31.

3:10.t: Quotations of Psalm 14:1-3, 53:1-3, 5:9, 140:3, 10:7, Isaiah 59:7-8 and Psalm 36:1.

3:22.t: "To all and on all who believe": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "to all who believe".

"Faith in Jesus Christ" (Greek pistis Iesou Christou): the KJV's "faith of Jesus Christ". The Greek can mean faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ; both are true in Paul. This translation follows the more traditional reading.

4:3.t: "Credited" (Greek logizomai): the KJV's "counted", "reckoned", "imputed", a bookkeeping word: to put to someone's account. The word occurs eleven times in this chapter. Abraham's faith was reckoned as righteousness.

4:19.t: "He did not consider his own body": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "he faced the fact that his body was as good as dead".

5:1.t: "We have peace": the KJV's reading. Many early manuscripts read "let us have peace"; the two Greek words differ by one letter.

5:11.t: "Reconciliation": the KJV's "the atonement", which in 1611 meant "at-one-ment", reconciliation (Greek katallage).
"Boast" (Greek kauchaomai): the KJV's "rejoice", "glory", "joy". The same word Paul condemns in 3:27, boasting in oneself, is here turned toward God.

5:12.t: Paul begins a comparison in verse 12 and completes it in verse 18; verses 13-17 explain it. The KJV marks verses 13-17 as a parenthesis.

"Because all sinned" (Greek eph ho pantes hemarton): the KJV's "for that all have sinned". Christians have understood this in different ways: that all sinned in Adam as their representative, that all inherited a sinful nature from him, or that all followed his example. Paul's main point is the parallel between Adam and Christ (5:18-19).

6:2.t: "By no means!": the KJV's "God forbid"; Greek me genoito, a strong denial, "May it never be!" See 3:4.

6:15.t: "By no means!": the KJV's "God forbid"; Greek me genoito, a strong denial, "May it never be!" See 3:4.

7:7.t: A quotation of Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21.

Readers have long debated who the "I" is: Paul as an unbeliever under the law, Paul as a believer still struggling with sin, or Israel's experience under the law told in the first person. The passage shows that the law, though good, cannot free anyone from sin's power; only Christ and the Spirit can (7:25-8:4).

8:1.t: "Who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here (compare 8:4).
"Condemnation" (Greek katakrima): the sentence and the penalty. "In Christ Jesus": Paul's favorite phrase for union with Christ.

8:2.t: "Me": the KJV's reading; some early manuscripts read "you".

8:11.t: "Because of His Spirit": the KJV's "by his Spirit"; manuscripts differ between "through" and "because of".

8:28.t: "All things work together for good": the KJV's reading. Some early manuscripts add "God" as the subject: "in all things God works for good".
"For good": not that every event is good, but that God works through all of them for the final good of those who love Him: to be made like His Son (8:29).

9:13.t: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated": see Malachi 1:2-3. In Hebrew idiom "love ... hate" can mean "choose ... not choose" (compare Luke 14:26).

9:27.t: A quotation of Isaiah 10:22-23 from the Greek. "Finish the work and cut it short in righteousness": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts have a shorter verse.

9:29.t: A quotation of Isaiah 1:9. "Lord of hosts": the KJV's "Lord of Sabaoth", Hebrew tseva'ot, "armies".

9:32.t: "Of the law": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

10:15.t: A quotation of Isaiah 52:7. "Who preach the gospel of peace and": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

10:17.t: "The word of God": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the word of Christ".

11:6.t: "But if it is by works, then it is no longer grace; otherwise work would no longer be work": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

11:8.t: A quotation of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10.

11:26.t: "All Israel will be saved": readers understand this as a future turning of the Jewish people as a whole to Christ, as the whole people of God (Jews and Gentiles together), or as the full number of believing Jews through history.

12:20.t: A quotation of Proverbs 25:21-22. "Burning coals on his head": perhaps a picture of the shame that leads to repentance.

13:9.t: Quotations of Exodus 20:13-17, Deuteronomy 5:17-21 and Leviticus 19:18. "You shall not bear false witness": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words here.

13:13.t: "Sexual immorality and debauchery": the KJV's "chambering and wantonness".

14:6.t: "And whoever does not regard the day does not regard it to the Lord": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

14:10.t: "Of Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "of God".

14:21.t: "Or to be offended, or made weak": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

15:9.t: Quotations of 2 Samuel 22:50 and Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1 and Isaiah 11:10.

15:19.t: Illyricum was a Roman province along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, in what is now Albania and the former Yugoslavia.

15:24.t: There is no record in the New Testament of Paul's reaching Spain; an early tradition says he did after his release from his first Roman imprisonment.

15:29.t: "Of the gospel": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

16:1.t: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth (Acts 18:18). Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome.

"Servant" (Greek diakonos): the word also means "deacon" (Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:8-13). Readers differ on whether Phoebe held the office of deacon or served in a general way; in either case Paul honors her ministry.

16:2.t: "Benefactor": the KJV's "succourer"; Greek prostatis, a patron or protector.

16:5.t: "Epenetus": the KJV's "Epaenetus". "The province of Achaia": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Asia".

16:7.t: "Junia": a woman's name, as the KJV and most early Christian writers took it; some later manuscripts and translations read the masculine "Junias". "Outstanding among the apostles": the KJV's "of note among the apostles". The Greek can mean that they were well known to the apostles, or that they were prominent apostles themselves, in the wider sense of missionaries sent out by the churches.

16:13.t: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21).

16:22.t: Tertius was Paul's scribe, writing the letter as Paul dictated.

16:23.t: "Director of public works": the KJV's "the chamberlain of the city"; Greek oikonomos, city treasurer or manager. An inscription found in Corinth names an Erastus who held a public office.

16:24.t: The KJV includes this verse; many early manuscripts do not have it.

16:25.t: Some manuscripts place these verses after 14:23 or 15:33.

1:1.t: "Servant" (Greek doulos): a slave, one wholly owned by a master. Paul uses it as a title of honor, like "servant of the LORD" for Moses and David.

1:3.t: "According to the flesh ... through the Spirit of holiness" (Greek kata sarka ... kata pneuma hagiosynes): two sides of who Jesus is: descended from David as a man, and shown with power to be God's Son by the resurrection. Sarx, "flesh", can mean real human nature with its weakness (see John 1:14); in Romans it often means human nature apart from God's Spirit (8:4-9).

1:5.t: "The obedience that comes from faith" (Greek hypakoen pisteos): the obedience that faith produces, or the obedience that is faith. Paul frames the letter with this phrase (16:26).

1:16.t: "Salvation" (Greek soteria): the same word means healing and rescue; see Acts 4:12. In Romans it means rescue from God's wrath (5:9) and the full restoration of life with Him.

1:18.t: "Wrath" (Greek orge): see John 3:36. God's wrath is not uncontrolled anger but His settled, just opposition to evil. Here it is shown in His "giving them over" to their own choices (1:24, 26, 28).

1:24.t: "Gave them over" (Greek paredoken): three times. God's judgment lets people go the way they have chosen.

1:26.t: Christians today read these verses differently. Most churches through history have taken them as Paul's teaching that sexual relations between people of the same sex are contrary to God's design; some recent interpreters argue that Paul had in view particular practices of his day, such as exploitation or idolatrous cults. "Natural ... unnatural" (Greek physikos ... para physin): according to nature, contrary to nature.

2:4.t: "Kindness ... forbearance ... patience" (Greek chrestotes, anoche, makrothymia): God's patience is not indifference; it is meant to lead to repentance.

2:13.t: "Declared righteous" (Greek dikaiothesontai): the KJV's "justified", to be declared righteous, as by a judge's verdict in court; Paul uses the word for God's verdict of righteousness on those who believe. See Matthew 12:37. Paul shows that hearing the law is not enough; in chapter 3 he shows that no one keeps it fully.

2:15.t: "Conscience" (Greek syneidesis): the inner awareness of right and wrong before God; see Acts 23:1.

2:29.t: "Circumcision of the heart": a picture of inward change from the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 10:16, 30:6, Jeremiah 4:4). "Written code" (Greek gramma): the KJV's "the letter", the law as written rules, in contrast to the Spirit's inner work (7:6, 2 Corinthians 3:6). "Praise ... from God": a play on "Jew", from Judah, whose name means "praise" (Genesis 29:35).

3:2.t: "Words" (Greek logia): the KJV's "oracles", God's revealed words, the Scriptures.

3:3.t: "Faithfulness" (Greek pistis): the same word as "faith". God's pistis is His trustworthiness and loyalty, like the Hebrew emunah and hesed.

3:20.t: "Works of the law" (Greek erga nomou): the deeds the law of Moses requires. Readers disagree on whether Paul means the law as a whole as a way of earning right standing, or especially the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. Either way, no one is justified by them.

3:24.t: "Justified" (Greek dikaioumenoi): declared righteous, acquitted, put right with God, as by a judge's verdict. See Matthew 12:37. "Freely" (Greek dorean): as a gift, without payment. "Redemption" (Greek apolytrosis): release by payment of a price, as a slave is set free.

3:25.t: "Sacrifice of atonement" (Greek hilasterion): the KJV's "propitiation". In the Greek Old Testament hilasterion is the "mercy seat", the lid of the ark where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15, Hebrews 9:5). The word carries both the turning away of God's wrath (propitiation) and the cleansing of sin (expiation). Christ is the place and the means of atonement. "Passed over" (Greek paresis): God had not yet fully punished sin, and the cross shows that He is just.

4:5.t: "Justifies the ungodly": a startling phrase. In the law, a judge who acquitted the guilty was condemned (Exodus 23:7, Proverbs 17:15). God can do it justly because of Christ (3:26).

4:25.t: "Delivered over to death for our sins ... raised to life for our justification": echoing Isaiah 53:5, 11-12.

5:2.t: "Boast" (Greek kauchaomai): the KJV's "rejoice", "glory", "joy". The same word Paul condemns in 3:27, boasting in oneself, is here turned toward God.

5:3.t: "Suffering ... perseverance ... character" (Greek thlipsis, hypomone, dokime): pressure, steady endurance, and proven character, tested like metal.

5:5.t: "God's love" (Greek he agape tou theou): God's love for us, poured out like a flood. Agape is not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good. See Matthew 5:43-44.

5:10.t: "Reconciled" (Greek katallasso): to change enemies into friends. God is the one who reconciles; humans are reconciled.

5:14.t: "Pattern" (Greek typos): the KJV's "figure", a type. Adam's act affected all who came after him, as Christ's does.

6:3.t: "Baptized into Christ Jesus ... into His death": baptism (Greek baptizo, to dip or immerse in water; see Matthew 3:6) pictures being plunged into Christ's death and rising with Him to new life.

6:6.t: "Old self" (Greek palaios anthropos): the KJV's "old man", what we were in Adam before union with Christ.

6:23.t: "Wages ... gift" (Greek opsonia ... charisma): opsonia was a soldier's pay, what is earned; charisma is a free gift of grace.

7:14.t: "Flesh" (Greek sarx, sarkinos): in Romans 7-8 "flesh" means human nature apart from God, weak and ruled by sin, not the physical body as such (see 1:3-4).

7:18.t: "Flesh" (Greek sarx, sarkinos): in Romans 7-8 "flesh" means human nature apart from God, weak and ruled by sin, not the physical body as such (see 1:3-4).

8:3.t: "To be a sin offering" (Greek peri hamartias): the KJV's "for sin". The phrase is used in the Greek Old Testament for the sin offering (Leviticus 5:6-7).

8:15.t: "Adoption to sonship" (Greek huiothesia): the KJV's "adoption". A Roman adopted son received full legal rights as heir. "Abba": Aramaic for "Father", the word a child used for his father, warm and respectful, which Jesus used in prayer; see Mark 14:36.

8:19.t: "Creation" (Greek ktisis): the KJV's "the creature", the whole created world, which suffers under the curse (Genesis 3:17-19) and will share in the coming freedom.

8:23.t: "Firstfruits" (Greek aparche): the first part of the harvest, the pledge of the rest. The Spirit now is the guarantee of the full redemption to come.

8:26.t: "Intercedes" (Greek hyperentynchanei): pleads on our behalf. The Spirit prays within us (8:26-27) and Christ prays for us at God's right hand (8:34).

8:29.t: "Foreknew ... predestined ... called ... justified ... glorified": Christians have understood God's foreknowledge and predestination differently: as God's choosing of His people beforehand, or as His knowing beforehand who would believe. Paul's purpose is assurance: what God has begun, He will complete; "glorified" is in the past tense as though already done.

8:37.t: "More than conquerors" (Greek hypernikomen): "we win an overwhelming victory".

9:5.t: "The Christ, who is God over all, forever praised": the KJV's reading. The Greek has no punctuation, and some read "Christ. God who is over all be forever praised!" The KJV reading, which calls Christ God, is the more natural reading of the Greek and was held by most early Christian writers.

9:6.t: This passage has long been central to debates about God's choosing (election). Some read it as God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation; others as His choice of peoples and their role in His plan (Israel, the Gentiles). Paul's aim is to show that God's word has not failed (9:6) and that God's mercy is free.

10:4.t: "The end of the law" (Greek telos nomou): telos means both "end" (termination) and "goal" (fulfillment). Christ is both: the goal the law pointed to, and the end of the law as a way to righteousness.

10:9.t: "Jesus is Lord" (Greek kyrion Iesoun): the earliest Christian confession. In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios translates the divine name, the LORD (compare 10:13, quoting Joel 2:32).

11:25.t: "Mystery" (Greek mysterion): not a puzzle but a secret once hidden and now revealed by God; see Matthew 13:11. "The full number of the Gentiles" (Greek to pleroma ton ethnon): the KJV's "the fulness of the Gentiles".

11:29.t: "Irrevocable" (Greek ametameleta): the KJV's "without repentance", meaning God does not change His mind or take back His gifts.

12:1.t: "True and proper worship" (Greek logike latreia): the KJV's "reasonable service". Logikos means rational, spiritual, fitting; latreia means priestly service or worship. The whole of life offered to God is worship.

12:2.t: "Transformed" (Greek metamorphousthe): changed in form, the word used of Jesus' transfiguration; see Matthew 17:2. "Conform" (Greek syschematizesthe): to be shaped by an outward pattern.

12:6.t: "Gifts" (Greek charismata): gifts of grace (charis). Compare 1 Corinthians 12.

12:9.t: "Love" (Greek agape) ... "devoted ... in love" (Greek philostorgoi ... philadelphia): Paul uses three words: agape, self-giving love; storge, family affection; and philadelphia, love for brothers and sisters.

13:1.t: "Governing authorities" (Greek exousiai hyperechousai): the KJV's "the higher powers", civil rulers. Paul wrote under Nero. Christians have long debated how this teaching applies when rulers command what God forbids; compare Acts 5:29.

13:4.t: "Servant" (Greek diakonos): the same word used for ministers of the gospel.

13:10.t: "Fulfillment" (Greek pleroma): love fills full what the law requires. Compare Matthew 22:37-40.

14:1.t: "Weak in faith": not weak in trusting Christ, but not yet convinced of the freedom faith brings in matters such as food and days. Paul calls both sides to welcome each other.

14:23.t: "Everything that does not come from faith is sin": to act against one's own conscience before God is sin, even in matters that are not wrong in themselves.

15:16.t: "Minister ... priestly duty" (Greek leitourgos ... hierourgounta): Paul describes his work as priestly service, offering the Gentiles to God as a sacrifice.

16:20.t: "Crush Satan under your feet": echoing Genesis 3:15.

16:26.t: "The obedience that comes from faith" (Greek hypakoen pisteos): the obedience that faith produces, or the obedience that is faith; see 1:5. Paul begins and ends the letter with this phrase.
